title: Thailand warns pet owners about potentially deadly tick-borne virus - Pattaya Mail

analysis.time: Thailand is raising awareness of SFTS, a tick-borne virus, as of November 3, 2026, with symptoms typically appearing within one to two weeks after exposure.
analysis.location_and_population: Thailand, specifically focusing on pet owners and individuals handling animals, including dogs, cats, and farm animals.
analysis.event: Thailand has recorded 10 cases and five deaths since 2019, including three cases and two deaths in the first nine months of 2026, according to the Department of Disease Control. The National Communicable Disease Committee has approved a draft measure to add SFTS to the country’s disease surveillance system.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Thailand has recorded 10 cases and five deaths since 2019, with three cases and two deaths reported in the first nine months of 2026. Severe cases can cause bleeding, organ failure, and death. There is currently no approved vaccine or specific antiviral treatment, making early medical attention crucial.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health officials advise pet owners to check animals regularly for ticks, use tick-control products, and avoid handling ticks with bare hands. Those working with animals or spending time outdoors should wear protective clothing and check their bodies after exposure. Anyone developing a high fever after a tick bite or close contact with animals should seek medical attention and inform doctors about the exposure.

analysis.brief_en: Thailand has issued a warning to pet owners about the potentially deadly tick-borne virus known as Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS). The Department of Disease Control reported 10 cases and five deaths since 2019, including three cases and two deaths in the first nine months of 2026. Health officials emphasize the importance of checking pets for ticks, using tick-control products, and avoiding direct contact with ticks. They also advise individuals working with animals or spending time outdoors to wear protective clothing and monitor their bodies for ticks. Symptoms of SFTS, which include high fever, fatigue, headache, muscle pain, nausea, and diarrhoea, typically appear within one to two weeks after exposure. Severe cases can lead to bleeding, organ failure, and death, with no approved vaccine or specific antiviral treatment currently available. The National Communicable Disease Committee has approved a draft measure to include SFTS in the country’s disease surveillance system, highlighting the growing concern over this virus. Pet owners are urged to take precautions to prevent tick bites and seek immediate medical attention if they or their pets develop a high fever following possible exposure.
analysis.summary_en: Thailand has issued a warning to pet owners about the potentially deadly tick-borne virus known as Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS). The Department of Disease Control reported 10 cases and five deaths since 2019, including three cases and two deaths in the first nine months of 2026. Health officials emphasize the importance of checking pets for ticks, using tick-control products, and avoiding direct contact with ticks. They also advise individuals working with animals or spending time outdoors to wear protective clothing and monitor their bodies for ticks. Symptoms of SFTS, which include high fever, fatigue, headache, muscle pain, nausea, and diarrhoea, typically appear within one to two weeks after exposure. Severe cases can lead to bleeding, organ failure, and death, with no approved vaccine or specific antiviral treatment currently available. The National Communicable Disease Committee has approved a draft measure to include SFTS in the country’s disease surveillance system, highlighting the growing concern over this virus. Pet owners are urged to take precautions to prevent tick bites and seek immediate medical attention if they or their pets develop a high fever following possible exposure.

title: Suspect Tick-Borne Infection if Fever or Chills Follow a Fall Foliage Outing - 아시아경제

analysis.time: The article was published on 03 November 2026 (KST). The event date is not explicitly stated in the evidence, but the focus is on fall foliage season, which typically occurs in September to November.
analysis.location_and_population: The location is Gwangju Special City, South Korea. The affected population includes residents and outdoor activity participants, particularly in areas with heavy outdoor activity such as trailheads, major tourist attractions, campgrounds, and recreational forests.
analysis.event: Gwangju Special City is concentrating its administrative efforts on preventing tick-borne infectious diseases, which peak in the fall. The article warns about suspect tick-borne infections if fever or chills follow a fall foliage outing.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 72.1% of cases of major tick-borne infectious diseases in South Korea over the past three years occurred from September to November. The article highlights the risk of scrub typhus and severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) during this period, with symptoms including fever, chills, rashes, and black scabs at the site of a chigger bite. SFTS causes symptoms such as fever, vomiting, and diarrhea.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Gwangju Special City is stepping up administrative measures to prevent the spread of these infectious diseases. It plans to distribute informational materials in rural areas and promote cooperation between medical institutions and public health centers to promptly determine whether patients with unexplained fevers in the fall have tick-borne infections.

analysis.brief_en: Gwangju Special City is intensifying efforts to prevent tick-borne infectious diseases, which peak during the fall season. The article highlights that 72.1% of major tick-borne disease cases in South Korea over the past three years occurred between September and November. It warns that symptoms such as fever and chills following outdoor activities like fall foliage outings may indicate a tick-borne infection. The city is focusing its guidance on areas with high outdoor activity, including trailheads, tourist attractions, campgrounds, and recreational forests. Additionally, it plans to distribute informational materials in rural areas and collaborate with medical institutions and public health centers to identify and manage tick-borne infections promptly. The article emphasizes the importance of preventive measures, such as wearing long clothing and avoiding direct contact with grass, to reduce the risk of tick exposure.
